posts.text:
NVIDIA: LITIGATION HISTORY AND THE SIDE C QUESTION, CONTINUED (3/3)

5. THE BAD TASTE SCENARIO, ASSESSED

The scenario: Jensen, or the institution he led, had a bad experience with this coverage in the 2000s, carriers that took premium and then fought payment, and concluded the product was not worth buying on the entity side. Assessed on the record, it is a genuinely available explanation, and it has real limits. Neither adopted nor dismissed here.

What supports it:

• Nvidia's only lived experience of its D&O tower, in the entire public record, was a fight. Its carriers raised exclusions, argued the claims were uninsurable restitution, argued the claims were outside the securities claims definition, and one carrier that had paid $1,845,000 sued the logic in reverse by seeking the money back. The company had to file its own lawsuit, in January 2005, and was still litigating the coverage in January 2007, years after the underlying claims arose. A decision maker who lived through that file has firsthand reason to doubt what a tower delivers when it is called.
• The fight was not trivial in context: defense costs alleged above $6.5M against a $25M tower, for a company that was then a small cap. The coverage dispute was material to the company of that era in a way it could never be to the company of 2026.

What limits it:

• The tower did pay. The primary $5M and the first $5M excess were alleged exhausted, which means they paid out; St. Paul's $1,845,000 was out the door before the clawback argument. The lived experience is therefore mixed, not a simple non payment story: the bottom of the tower performed, the upper layers resisted, and the 2007 ruling kept Nvidia's coverage arguments alive rather than killing them.
• The disputed claims were bankruptcy creditor claims arising from an acquisition, an unusual underlying matter at the edge of the policy definitions, not a securities class action and not a settlement. Whatever skepticism the episode teaches attaches to contested edge claims and defense cost fights; it says little about how a tower performs on the standard securities claim, which is the risk Side C exists for, and which Nvidia has never tendered because it has never settled one.
• No document connects the 2005 to 2007 experience to any later placement decision. No statement by any Nvidia officer, no broker account, and no reporting links the A only structure of 2026 to the coverage fight of 2005. The two events sit more than twenty years apart, across a complete change of scale, and the record contains nothing in between.
• The scenario also has to compete with the timing problem that governs every explanation in this file: until the placement and restructure history surfaces, no motive, mundane or otherwise, can be dated or tested.

Net assessment: the bad taste scenario is a plausible human explanation that the record neither confirms nor excludes. It is weaker than it first sounds, because the tower substantially performed, and it is stronger than a pure invention, because the fight was real, expensive, and Nvidia's only documented experience of the product.

6. PREMIUM: ESTIMATE ONLY

ESTIMATE. This entire section is an estimate constructed from market benchmarks. No source anywhere states Nvidia's actual D&O premium, for the reported Side A program or for any prior year; EDGAR, trade press, and general searches for any Nvidia premium figure returned nothing. Any figure attributed to Nvidia's program in commentary should be treated as invented unless it cites a filing.

• Market backdrop: D&O pricing in 2025 and 2026 sits at roughly 2019 levels after several years of declines, well below the 2020 to 2022 hard market peak, in a market with abundant capacity competing for business. Any premium saving taken now was taken at the cheapest point in the cycle to buy the coverage skipped. Grade: VERIFIED as to the published broker index data underlying that description; the application to Nvidia is ESTIMATE.
• Full ABC

NVIDIA: LITIGATION HISTORY AND THE SIDE C QUESTION, CONTINUED (2/3)

3. ADJACENT MATTERS, IN THEIR OWN LANES

None of the following is a Side C event. Each is recorded because it touches the insurance record, and each is graded in its proper lane so it cannot be miscounted as entity coverage evidence.

3.1 THE 3DFX ADVERSARY PROCEEDINGS (BANKRUPTCY CREDITOR CLAIMS)

Arising from Nvidia's December 2000 purchase of 3dfx assets for $70M plus 1,000,000 Nvidia shares, the 3dfx Chapter 11 trustee and other claimants sued Nvidia, its subsidiary, and its directors and officers, alleging insufficient consideration, fraud on creditors, interference with contract, breach of fiduciary duty, and de facto merger. The estate claims were compromised in a Settlement Agreement dated November 1, 2005, under which Nvidia agreed to pay $5,524,759.77 to a senior claims account and $25,000,000 to a general claims account; the agreement's payment language runs from Nvidia and does not state what portion, if any, the D&O tower funded. The trustee's fraudulent conveyance theory ended in Nvidia's favor when the Ninth Circuit affirmed on November 6, 2014 that Nvidia did not pay less than fair market value. Sources: executed settlement agreement (SEC exhibit copy); Ninth Circuit memorandum disposition. Grade: VERIFIED as to the settlement terms; the insurance allocation is NOT FOUND. These proceedings are the underlying claims in the coverage fight told in full in Section 4.

3.2 THE DERIVATIVE SUITS (SIDE A LANE)

• 2002 derivative actions: three actions followed the February 2002 accounting announcement. The Delaware action, Guttman v. Huang, was dismissed with prejudice on May 5, 2003 for failure to plead demand futility (823 A.2d 492); the two California actions were dismissed in September 2003 at plaintiffs' request. No carrier payment reported. Sources: Nvidia Q3 FY2003 10-Q; the Guttman opinion. Grade: VERIFIED.
• Options backdating derivative settlement, 2008: Nvidia's Form 8-K dated November 10, 2008 states the settlement terms for the stockholder derivative lawsuits over historical stock option practices, including "an $8.0 million cash payment by our insurance carrier to NVIDIA", corporate governance changes, and the CEO amending options to add $3.5M of exercise price or cancel equivalent intrinsic value. Grade: VERIFIED. Lane discipline: a carrier paying settlement consideration to the company in a derivative case is Side A territory. It proves a D&O carrier paid real money in an Nvidia matter; it is not entity securities coverage evidence and is not counted as such anywhere in this report. Background: the audit committee review began in June 2006, Nvidia restated fiscal 2004 to 2006 and earlier periods for incorrect option measurement dates (aggregate non cash charge ultimately $127M), and in November 2007 the SEC closed its backdating investigation with no enforcement action. Grade: VERIFIED.
• 2019 crypto derivative actions: the federal consolidated derivative case (No. 4:19-cv-00341-HSG, filed January 18, 2019) and two Delaware actions (filed September 24, 2019) were stayed pending the securities appeal; per Nvidia's Q3 FY2026 10-Q the federal case was administratively closed on February 22, 2022 and had not been reopened. No derivative settlement and no carrier payment is reported for any of them. Grade: VERIFIED. Lane: Side A exposure that never matured into a payment.
• A 2026 derivative complaint against the board over AI model copyright and biometric privacy allegations was covered by specialist press on August 10, 2026; no settlement or insurance information attaches to it in any source located. Grade: REPORTED. Lane: Side A.

Overnight, Reuters reported that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's own general counsel and chief marketing officer in writing that his interactions with Alice Huang and Megaspeed were standard business dealings, the House chairs' 8 p.m. deadline for his written acceptance of the December 1 interview passed with nothing public, and a filings-based reconstruction put $5,353 million of Nvidia's formerly Singapore-billed revenue with China and Hong Kong headquartered buyers. Super Micro denied on the record that Megaspeed was ever its customer, a sitting administration official argued Huang should have been warned the way a congressman once was, and the street kept repricing the overhang: HSBC cut its target by more than half, and a billionaire holder said he will make no further investment in Nvidia without Huang.

THE ASSURANCES INSIDE NVIDIA

• Reuters reported today that Huang misled several of Nvidia's leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang: in two separate messages in October 2026, and in other messages, Huang told Nvidia leaders including Teter and Wagonfeld that his interactions with Alice Huang and Megaspeed reflected "standard business dealings with customers" and affirmed the routine nature of his interactions with Megaspeed, according to two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence reviewed by Reuters. Reuters reviewed several October exchanges, on condition of not quoting them verbatim, and is the first to report this correspondence.
• The people said Huang gave similar assurances in the autumn of 2025, in response to press queries; Reuters did not review the 2025 exchanges. Huang also discussed taking legal action against The New York Times over its October 2025 article drawing attention to his public meetings with Alice Huang; neither Huang nor Nvidia filed a lawsuit and the Times received no legal demand.
• Reuters verified photos showing the pair together in the US, China and elsewhere dating back to December 2023; when the relationship became intimate remains unclear. Teter did not respond to comment requests, Wagonfeld did not immediately respond, and Huang's representative and Nvidia declined to comment. This is Reuters' own reporting: the misled parties here are Nvidia's own senior executives, not investigators, and Reuters offers no evidence about what Huang knew of the intelligence or export-control concerns.

THE DEADLINE PASSES IN SILENCE

• The 8 p.m. ET November 13 deadline in the three chairs' November 12 letter, for Huang to confirm in writing that he would sit for the December 1 closed-door transcribed interview, passed with no public confirmation, refusal, subpoena issuance, or committee statement in the case record's coverage through about 10:16 p.m. ET. The only post addressing the deadline's outcome in the window noted that the deadline came and went and that no confirmation from Huang had been made public. That is the public record only: whether a written confirmation was delivered through non-public channels is unverified, and nothing public appeared on Tim Teter's December 2 confirmation either. The chairs' stated next step, a House Foreign Affairs Committee subpoena to compel, is now in play.
• Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a House Intelligence Committee member, said on CNBC on November 13, in words verified against the full transcript of the clip: "We want more facts. We want to understand exactly the timeline here and the information at hand." He said the official response from Huang had not come in yet, that three committees with jurisdiction had asked Huang to testify and "threatened yesterday to issue subpoenas to get the information we need," and that the key question is whether advanced chips were diverted to China. quoted.text:
Bitcoin fell 19% into the biggest IPO ever. Now it's down 18% heading into the second biggest.

SpaceX raised $75B when it went public on June 12. In the 50 days before it listed, Bitcoin dropped 19%. Anthropic plans to raise up to $64B when it lists next week, and Bitcoin is down 18% over the same stretch. Overlay the two and they look almost the same.

What happened after the SpaceX IPO is the notable part. Bitcoin bottomed 18 days after the listing, then recovered all the way. By Day 100, it was above where it started.

Bitcoin around the SpaceX IPO:

Day -50 to IPO day: -19%
Low (Day +18): -25%
Day +50: still -20%
Around Day +70: a sharp rally
Day +100: +3.7%

From the IPO-day close to Day +100, Bitcoin gained 28%. From the low, it gained 39%.

The takeaway is that the selling came in the run-up to the listing. The bottom had effectively happened by the IPO, and the recovery came relatively shortly after, and it came all at once.

If Anthropic follows the same pattern, most of the drawdown is behind us, and it could reverse quickly over the next couple of months. And Bitcoin is sitting right at its 200-week moving average.

Map the SpaceX path onto today's price and you get roughly $90k by late February. Markets rarely follow a comparison like this exactly. But we remain very constructive on both the technicals and the fundamentals heading into 2027, and it's not hard to imagine what the narrative would be if anything close to this plays out.

posts.name: The All-In Podcast
posts.text:
David Sacks: Jensen Huang’s Exit Is a Big Win for China

“You ask the question ‘Cui bono? Who benefits?’ It's China. China benefits from this.

Jensen's been working on GPUs for over three decades. The chips are being improved rapidly. There's a new generation of chips that come out every year.

And it's that momentum, it's the ability to tape out a brand-new chip that's several times more powerful than last year's chip, that's the real advantage.

It's Nvidia’s competitive advantage, and it's America's advantage. It's the momentum, it's the dynamism.

People get way too hung up on some chip that was state-of-the-art four years ago. That's not where the United States has the advantage. It's that we are rapidly iterating, and we keep coming up with better and more powerful chips.

Now, let's take into account what's just happened. Do you think that Nvidia is going to lose a tempo or two? Absolutely.

Nvidia’s success was based on the ability to tape out a new chip design every year, and Jensen is fundamental to that rapid progress, the same way that Elon is fundamental to the rapid progress at SpaceX or Tesla.

And if you take him out of the picture, there's just nobody comparable.

It means that Nvidia’s chips will not continue to advance at the same pace. That's really good news for Huawei because they will catch up a lot faster.”

Jensen poussé dehors, ce que ça change pour le trade IA

Si vous êtes intéressé par le trade IA vous voulez peut-être vous asseoir avant de lire ça

J'étais assez remonté, alors j'ai pris le temps de tout poser à plat

1. Pourquoi il part

Let's recap, Dimanche, Jensen reconnaît une liaison avec une ex-dirigeante de son client Megaspeed, soupçonnée "d'espionner" pour Pékin. Le conseil ouvre une enquête et lui renouvelle sa confiance. Mercredi, le NYT rapporte une autre relation, avec une de ses direct reports. Le conseil se réunit le soir même et jeudi il est dehors. Avec 3,6 % du capital et pas de supervote à la Zuckerberg, il ne pouvait pas résister

On parle quand même d'un conseil qui a moins d'1% des shares qui le soutient le dimanche et le sort quatre jours plus tard, avant la fin de sa propre enquête. Criminel

2. Le produit reste intact à moyen terme

Le carnet couvre 12 à 24 mois, le consensus voit une demande 50 % au-dessus de l'offre et Vera Rubin monte en production. Même le débat sur le moat CUDA tué par l'IA est surjoué pour Morgan Stanley, Nvidia garde plus de 80 % des revenus du marché...

3. La fin de la banque de l'IA ?

Nvidia réinjecte dans l'écosystème une bonne part de ses 50 à 60 Md$ de cash-flow trimestriel, et une simple pause peut retirer 50 Md$ du système. Le plan à 500 Md$ annoncé en août avec six prêteurs n'a débouché sur aucun prêt, et l'un d'eux pense à sortir selon le NYT. 

Colette Kress, CEO par intérim, s'était battue cet été pour ramener la garantie du data center OpenAI de l'Ohio de 250 à moins de 120 Md$. Les engagements signés devraient tenir, mais les petits neoclouds, qui vivaient des nouveaux deals, sont pour moi les grands perdants, d'ailleurs ils se font massacrer

4. Washington et l'export

C'est ce qui semble le plus embêtant. Jensen menait deux combats, la Chine & l'open weight. Sans lui, trois projets de loi sur les puces avancent dans la loi de défense à voter avant fin décembre. La Justice mène une enquête pénale sur Megaspeed, qui a acheté plus de 4 Md$ de puces. UBS et New Street voient environ 10 % du CA exposé à des règles plus dures

5. Les talents

Ce risque-là ne se mesurera qu'à moyen terme. Jensen avait 60 direct reports et aucun plan de succession connu. Beaucoup d'ingénieurs seniors sont déjà financièrement libres et restaient d'abord pour lui. S'ils partent avec leurs équipes, ce sera bien plus grave, un peu comme chez Google avec le départ des Sr. Fellows

Mon humble avis

Aucun conseil n'aurait vraiment laisser passer la relation avec un direct report je l'entends. Mais le virer en une nuit, sans successeur, était une erreur, et Nvidia comme ses actionnaires vont la payer. @altcap et @GavinSBaker  ont écrit au conseil pour garder son retour sur la table, et la pétition pour le réintégrer dépasse 70 000 signatures, Musk compris

Sur le timing, je n'ai aucune preuve, mais j'ai du mal à croire au hasard. Washington avait le dossier depuis des mois, avec un mémo classifié dès mai selon Axios, et l'article du NYT qui lance l'affaire sort cinq jours avant les midterms. À l'heure où le compute est devenu le nouveau charbon, Jensen pesait trop lourd pour certains, avec ses avis tranchés sur l'open weight et la Chine. Trump, lui, l'a poussé à se battre selon le NYT

À 163$, après six semaines de baisse d'affilée, environ 10 fois les bénéfices 2027, le marché a déjà beaucoup pricé. Je ne crois pas pour autant au rebond rapide. Sur un an, je vois un fournisseur plus prudent et un titre plafonné, sans CEO permanent ni visibilité sur l'enquête export

Jeudi, les particuliers ont acheté pour 111 M$ nets de titres dans la première demi-heure, un record. Et comme si rien n'avait changé. Apple, après Jobs, a glissé de 17 à 9 fois les bénéfices avant de remonter, mais chaque boîte est BIEN différente

Tout ça dessert le trade IA dans son ensemble et donne du mou à la Chine, qui a probablement commencé à swap vers ses propres puces Huawei

Prochain rendez-vous mardi 17/11, première

Bon, j'ai essayé de résumer ce qu'on sait sur l'histoire entre Jensen et Alice Huang

L'histoire a continué cette nuit et c'est compliqué de tout suivre

1. Jensen Huang a reconnu une infidélité dans un mémo aux salariés : « I was unfaithful to my wife »

2.D'après le renseignement américain, Alice Huang (dirigeante ou ex-dirigeante de Megaspeed, client de Nvidia basé à Singapour) aurait été recrutée par le ministère chinois de la Sécurité d'État

Inflation Cycle Playbook (Livestream Reply)

Friday’s livestream laid out the full inflation cycle playbook: why headline and core are rising together, why nominal demand running near 6% against a 4% policy rate is an amplifier rather than a brake, and why the inflation swap market is still pricing a deceleration the data does not support. We walked through where each economy sits on the cycle clock, what term premium and the short end are telling us about the next leg in rates, how factor flows show equities positioned for AI momentum rather than macro risk, and the redundancy plan for headline and core moving in any combination. The 60/40 study closes the loop: more than half of this year’s nominal return has been eaten by inflation, which is exactly the setup that preceded 2022. posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
The last 20 years have been a fascinating test of capitalism and the narratives around it.

The GFC backlash was deserved. Banks made reckless and often predatory loans, then got bailed out. That was corporatism at its worst, and I was critical of it at the time. Some of you might remember I was basically in favor of Keynesianism on steroids back then, because the economy had a massive demand hole to fill.

Covid was different. Lockdowns caused supply shocks, and then we met those shocks with trillions in fiscal stimulus. Too much spending chasing too little supply. High inflation was the predictable result. That was big government at work trying to fix a problem and making it worse in many ways. Yet many people still blame “capitalism” for the outcome.

Two very different crises. Same scapegoat. It’s a good reminder that we all fit the facts to the story we already believe.
